provenance.notes: Mech family batch, quote archetype. Rural and suburban, urgent and nearly invisible online. County permit and inspection rules vary, so copy uses bracketed placeholders and never states a requirement. No equipment or tank brands. Ranges are planning figures.

pageStructurePlus.section: How often to pump your septic tank
pageStructurePlus.contains: Tank size, people in the house, garbage disposal use, the date of the last pump-out, and a reminder sign-up for the next one
pageStructurePlus.why: Most septic owners have no idea when the tank was last pumped. A plain schedule turns a once-a-crisis customer into a booked pump-out every few years.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Soggy ground or bright green strips over the leach field, slow drains through the house, gurgling, sewage smell in the yard, and backups in the lowest drain
pageStructurePlus.why: Owners search symptoms before they search for a company. Naming the signs plainly tells them whether it's a pump-out or a drain field problem worth a visit.

pageStructurePlus.contains: What a transfer or point-of-sale septic inspection covers, bracketed county and lender requirements, how long before closing to book, and a sample inspection report
pageStructurePlus.why: Realtors and buyers need the septic inspection done on a deadline. A clear page with a sample report wins the booking from the agent's phone.

pageStructurePlus.section: New septic system and perc test path
pageStructurePlus.contains: Soil and perc test, county permit, system design, conventional versus mound or aerobic treatment unit, install timeline and final county inspection
pageStructurePlus.why: Rural land buyers and new builders start from zero. The installer who lays out the steps gets the whole job, from the perc test to the final inspection.

pageStructurePlus.section: Sewer line camera and trenchless options
pageStructurePlus.contains: Camera inspection of the sewer lateral, roots and collapsed clay or cast iron pipe, trenchless lining versus digging, and who owns the line up to the city main
pageStructurePlus.why: Town homeowners with a backup want to know if the yard gets torn up. Showing trenchless options and the camera footage decides the job.

designDirections.name: County Road
designDirections.bestFor: Family-run septic pumping outfits with a truck or two serving rural roads and small towns
designDirections.headlineSample: Septic pumping and repair across {City} and the county roads
designDirections.whyItFits: Brick, linen and a slab display face feel like a family name painted on a pump truck, which is exactly the trust a rural septic owner is looking for.

designDirections.name: Backup Hotline
designDirections.bestFor: Septic and sewer contractors that answer backups, alarms and overflowing tanks as well as quoted installs
designDirections.headlineSample: Septic backup or sewer line clog in {City}? Call now
designDirections.whyItFits: The family's own combo, even for a quote-led trade: a sewage backup is an emergency first and a quote second, and mono labels suit tank sizes and service fees.

designDirections.name: Perc to Permit
designDirections.bestFor: Septic installers designing new systems for rural builds, land buyers and drain field replacements
designDirections.headlineSample: New septic systems in {City}, from perc test to final inspection
designDirections.whyItFits: Olive and a bookish serif slow the reader down for a long, permit-heavy decision where the steps matter more than speed.

openers.line: {Business Name} is on the map with a pump truck in the profile shot and no website. When someone's septic alarm goes off, they want to see who comes to their road before they dial.
openers.hook: Open their Maps listing and confirm there is no Website button. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: The septic site that listing could link to: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your listing points to Facebook, where the septic posts sit between everything else on the feed. A buyer needing a septic inspection before closing wants a form and a sample report.
openers.hook: Tap their Website link and confirm it lands on Facebook. Note the latest septic or sewer post.
openers.linkLine: A septic page made for buyers and realtors: {demo-link}

openers.line: The septic site on your listing still has a free-host banner and a dead contact page. Rural customers already struggle to find a septic company, and that page makes it harder.
openers.hook: Open the site and look for a builder banner, an old copyright year or a dead form. Note which one you found.
openers.linkLine: Same septic company, current and easy on a phone: {demo-link}

openers.line: On my phone, your septic page shows a desktop layout and a number I couldn't tap. Someone with sewage coming up a floor drain is holding a phone, not sitting at a computer.
openers.hook: Only if they have a site. Load it on a phone and note whether the number taps and text is readable. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Your septic site rebuilt for a phone: {demo-link}

openers.angle: No way to request a pump-out
openers.line: There's no way to book a septic pump-out with {Business Name} except calling. Most people remember the tank on a Sunday night and would rather send the address and tank size.
openers.hook: Check the listing, the social pages and any site for a request form. If there is none, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: A pump-out request that asks for tank size and lid location: {demo-link}

openers.line: A lot of septic inspection calls come from realtors racing a closing date. A page with the inspection steps and a request form gets the agent's booking without three phone calls.
openers.hook: Look for any mention of real estate, home sale or transfer inspections in posts or reviews. Quote it if you find it.
openers.linkLine: A septic inspection page built for closing deadlines: {demo-link}

openers.line: One review says you came out on a holiday weekend when the septic backed up into the basement. That's the story the next panicked owner needs to read, and it's stuck on the map.
openers.hook: Read their reviews and copy one specific phrase about a backup, a pump-out or a drain field. Quote it back if they reply.
openers.linkLine: Those septic reviews on a page owners actually read: {demo-link}

openers.line: Spring thaw and heavy rain are when saturated drain fields start backing up across {City}. The septic company that's easy to find that week takes the calls.
openers.hook: Use this in late winter or before the rainy season. Name the season in the reply.
openers.linkLine: Ready before the wet-season septic calls: {demo-link}

openers.line: Septic alarms and sewer backups don't wait for business hours. If that call rolls to a full mailbox, the owner keeps dialling until another pump truck answers.
openers.hook: Call their listed number after hours. If it goes to a full or generic voicemail, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: A septic backup request that works after hours: {demo-link}

openers.line: Saw you're looking for a CDL driver for the pump truck. Drivers check whether a septic company looks steady before they switch, and there's nothing online to show them.
openers.hook: Only if they posted a hiring note, a story or a truck sign. Note the date of the post.
openers.linkLine: A septic company page with a careers section: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your reviews mention septic work out in townships well past {City}, but nothing tells someone on a farm road near {Neighborhood} your truck goes there. That's exactly where septic lives.
openers.hook: Find townships or roads named in reviews or posts. Use the most rural one.
openers.linkLine: A septic page for each township you serve: {demo-link}

openers.line: If {Business Name} offers payments on a new drain field or septic system, say so on a page. That's a number nobody budgets for, and they put off calling until it's worse.
openers.hook: Only if they mention financing somewhere: a post, a review, the truck. If not, skip this angle.
openers.linkLine: Septic payment options, explained before the quote: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your septic installer registration is on the county or state list, but owners never look there. Putting it on a page is the quickest way to stand out from the guy with a backhoe and no permit.
openers.hook: Look them up on the state or county installer list. Note that a record exists; never quote a number you didn't see.
openers.linkLine: Registration, insurance and permits on one septic page: {demo-link}

openers.line: Out here everyone knows your septic truck, so maybe you've never needed a site. New people moving onto acreage don't know anyone yet, and they search.
openers.hook: Look for reviews from new arrivals or posts about new builds. Quote it back.
openers.linkLine: Where newcomers would find your septic company: {demo-link}

openers.line: That {specific recent job} you posted is a clean septic install, level tank and tidy backfill. A buyer comparing installers should see that first, not a feed of road shots.
openers.hook: Pick their newest finished job and name it exactly: tank, drain field, mound or sewer line, and the township if tagged.
openers.linkLine: That septic job, front and centre: {demo-link}

sequence.dm2:

IF YES:
"What did you think of it?"
 → let them talk, don't fill the silence
"It's not ads and not a lead service, it's a site you own. The build runs {Build Range} depending on how many township and service pages you want, then {Care Range} a month for hosting and changes. For your outfit I'd say about {Build Price}, less than one drain field repair."
"Could I walk you through it for ten minutes, maybe early one morning before the first pump-out?"

CLOSE:
"I'll send a one-page scope and a deposit invoice. When it clears I start, and the inspection page goes live first so realtors can find you."

objections.objection: Everyone out here already knows us.
objections.handler: "The locals do. New owners on acreage and realtors from the city don't, and they search. The site is for the people who haven't met your truck yet."

objections.objection: We're booked weeks out on pump-outs already.
objections.handler: "Then the site does triage. Routine pump-outs book themselves into open slots online, and the phone stays free for backups and installs."

objections.objection: I can't put prices on septic work. Every system is different.
objections.handler: "We won't. The page explains how you quote, asks for tank size and the last pump date, and you price it. Nothing goes up you haven't approved."

objections.objection: Most of our work comes from realtors.
objections.handler: "Then the inspection page is for them. Agents book the septic inspection online with the closing date, and you stop playing phone tag."

objections.objection: My wife handles the office and the Facebook page.
objections.handler: "Good, she'll like this. The site takes the bookings she's writing down by hand, and she can still post to Facebook whenever she wants."
"{Build Range}. For you, about {Build Price}, because it's a pump-out request, an inspection page and a few township pages. One new system install pays for it many times over."

bullets: Peg the build to a fraction of one drain field repair. Septic owners think in pump-outs and installs, not web hours.
The home-sale inspection page is the wedge with realtors; price it as its own line.
Quote pumping, inspection, new system and sewer line pages separately. Each has a different buyer.
Never state a county rule, setback or inspection requirement; use bracketed fields the owner fills.
Township pages matter more than city pages here. Price per township with jobs behind it.
Pumping-only outfits need a lighter scope than installers who design systems. Size it to what they sell.

whatElseYouSell.name: Review requests after each pump-out
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "After the tank is pumped and the lids are back, the owner gets a text asking how the septic crew did. Rural reviews are rare, so each one counts."

whatElseYouSell.name: Google profile upkeep for septic service
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Your Google profile lists every township you cover, posts each septic install and answers questions, so the map shows a company that's active on those roads."
whatElseYouSell.when: Day 30, once the site is live.

whatElseYouSell.name: Realtor septic inspection packet
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A one-page packet for every listing agent in the county explaining the septic inspection, how far ahead to book and the online request."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 2, before the spring selling season.

whatElseYouSell.name: Pump truck lettering artwork
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Your pump truck is the best-known vehicle on every back road. Clean lettering with the site and number makes it work as a septic billboard."
whatElseYouSell.when: Right after launch, or when a truck is repainted.

whatElseYouSell.name: Septic care mailer to rural routes
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A postcard to rural routes on what not to flush, how often to pump and the warning signs at the drain field, with the septic number on the front."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 3, mailed to routes where they already pump.

whatElseYouSell.name: Local Services Ads for septic
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Septic searches are few but urgent. A licence-checked ad catches the backup search before the owner scrolls to a company two counties away."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 3, once reviews are flowing and documents are current.

whatElseYouSell.name: New-build and land buyer outreach page
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A page and leave-behind for land agents and rural builders that explains the perc test and septic permit path, ending in a design request."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 4, for installers who design new systems.

withoutAI.route: Excavators who dig for the septic installer
withoutAI.whoPays: The excavation contractor, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "Who digs the drain field trenches when you're not running the machine? That excavator needs a site, and your new septic page links to theirs."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Septic and excavation crews share almost every install and already refer each other.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The land agents who book your septic inspections sell acreage with wells, septic and outbuildings. Their sites rarely explain any of it."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Rural agents need specialised listing pages, and the septic company is a trusted vendor.

withoutAI.whoPays: The well contractor, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "Every rural lot needs a well and a septic system, and the setback between them matters. The well driller you work beside needs a site too."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Wells and septic go into the same new builds, and both owners already send each other land buyers.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The builders whose new homes you put septic systems under show finished kitchens, not the land prep. Your introduction gets me in to build their site."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Builders spend more on sites than trades do, and the septic installer is a voice they trust.

withoutAI.route: Portable toilet and grease trap haulers
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The hauler who takes your overflow or pumps grease traps runs a different service on the same trucks. They need a catalogue-style site."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Haulers and septic firms share disposal sites and drivers, and refer work back and forth.

withoutAI.route: Campgrounds and rural venues on septic
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The campgrounds and wedding barns you pump every season need booking sites far more than septic does. You're already on their property."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Rural hospitality owners trust the septic vendor who keeps them open, and their sites are usually poor.

withAI.route: Listing description writer for land agents
withAI.pitchLine: "An assistant drafts acreage listings from the agent's notes, with well, septic and access described accurately and flagged for the agent to confirm."
withAI.whyItWorks: Land listings are hard to write and septic details are where agents get caught out.

withAI.pitchLine: "The excavator who digs your septic jobs loses site-prep bids to slow callbacks. Automatic follow-up drafted in their voice fixes it."
withAI.whyItWorks: It's configuration of a tool you've built, and the septic owner's introduction carries trust.

withAI.pitchLine: "Rural build clients make dozens of choices. An assistant tracks them and flags the ones that affect the septic, like extra bathrooms or a basement bar."
withAI.whyItWorks: Builders lose time to selection changes, and fixture counts change the septic design.

withAI.route: Water test report explainer for well drillers
withAI.pitchLine: "Well owners get lab reports full of numbers. An assistant writes a plain summary the driller reviews and sends, with any septic setback concern noted."
withAI.whyItWorks: Drillers field the same questions on every report, and septic and wells share the same customers.

withAI.pitchLine: "Campers report a smelly or slow restroom at night. An assistant logs it, suggests the first checks and books the septic pump-out if the tank is due."
withAI.whyItWorks: Campgrounds can't afford a closed restroom on a busy weekend, and the septic company gets the call.

withAI.route: Route planner for the hauling company
withAI.pitchLine: "An assistant plans each day's grease trap and portable toilet stops by location and disposal site, and drafts the customer texts."
withAI.whyItWorks: Haulers burn fuel on bad routes, and the septic owner knows exactly which haulers to introduce.

softwareAI.name: Septic call catcher for the truck
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Calls you miss with the hose running get a text back asking whether sewage is in the house or the alarm is sounding, so backups get called first and pump-outs get booked."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Day 30. Needs the business number forwarded and the wording approved.

softwareAI.name: Pump-out due-date reminders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every septic customer gets a text when their tank is due by size and household, with open pump-out days to tap. Years of repeat work, booked automatically."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs the customer list with tank sizes and last pump dates, even rough ones.

softwareAI.name: Tank and lid location map
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every property's septic tank, lids, drain field and distribution box pinned on a map with notes, so the next driver doesn't spend an hour probing the yard."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs drivers to drop a pin and a shot at each job for a season.

softwareAI.name: Septic inspection report builder
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Tick through tank condition, baffles, levels and drain field checks on a phone, and a clean septic inspection report goes to the realtor before the truck leaves."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their inspection checklist and the county's required form fields, if any.

softwareAI.name: Reply drafts for septic reviews
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A plain-spoken reply drafted for each review that mentions the backup, the pump-out or the new drain field, ready to approve from the cab."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2, with review requests running. Needs ten past replies. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Realtor booking portal for septic inspections
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Agents book the septic inspection against the closing date, upload the seller's records and download the report, without a single phone call to the office."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their inspection slots and report format.

softwareAI.name: Night backup line for septic and sewer
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It answers a sewer backup call at night, tells the owner to stop running water, asks about the alarm and books the first slot, waking the owner only for sewage in the house."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their after-hours rules and fee wording. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Pumping route planner
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Each day's pump-outs ordered by road and disposal site with truck capacity counted, so the driver isn't crossing the county twice."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs truck capacities, disposal sites and a few weeks of jobs.

softwareAI.name: Records reader for old septic permits
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Upload the scanned county septic permit or as-built drawing and it pulls out the tank size, install year and field layout for the job file."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs a stack of past permits. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer; a tech checks every extraction.

softwareAI.name: Sewer camera clip report
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Mark roots, offsets and breaks by footage on the sewer camera run and send the owner a short report with stills and the repair options."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4, for firms with a camera. Needs two past camera jobs and their wording.

softwareAI.name: Q&A assistant for septic owners
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It answers 'how often should I pump' and 'is this smell normal' from the septic company's own notes, and books a visit when the answer is 'come look'."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs their FAQ notes and service area. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Install quote builder with system options
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Build a repair, a drain field replacement and a full new septic system option with permit costs, and the owner signs the one they choose."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs their pricing for common septic jobs and system types.

softwareAI.name: Spoken notes to septic invoice
softwareAI.pitchLine: "The driver says the gallons pumped, lids dug and any baffle issue into the phone, and the septic invoice and service note are drafted."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5. Needs their invoice template and price list. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Aerobic unit service contract tracker
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every aerobic septic unit under contract with its required service visits, the county report due dates and the last findings, all in one place."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6, for firms servicing aerobic units. Needs the contract list and any county reporting rules.

softwareAI.name: Deposit and permit-stage billing for installs
softwareAI.pitchLine: "A new septic install bills a deposit at signing, a draw at county approval and the balance after final inspection, each sent on time without the office chasing it."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs their draw schedule and payment account.

softwareAI.name: Drain field failure risk notes
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It reads a year of pump-out notes and flags systems with high levels, solids carryover or soggy fields, so the septic owner can offer a check before a failure."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 7. Needs a year of service notes. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer; it never predicts a failure date.

softwareAI.name: Disposal log and manifest tracker
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every load of septage logged by truck, gallons and disposal site, with the monthly manifest ready for the regulator or the treatment plant."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 7. Needs their current manifest forms and disposal sites.

softwareAI.name: Spring thaw alert to past septic customers
softwareAI.pitchLine: "When heavy rain or the thaw is forecast around {City}, past septic customers get a text on easing water use and the number to call if drains slow."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 7. Needs the customer list and a weather feed.

softwareAI.name: Driver training notes from senior pumpers
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Your senior driver talks through finding buried lids, reading levels and spotting a failing septic field, and it becomes a how-to library for new drivers."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 8. Needs a driver willing to record. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: CDL driver applicant screen
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Applicants for the pump truck say whether they hold the right CDL class, can handle septage and work early mornings, before anyone calls them."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Whenever they post a hiring note. Needs must-haves and pay range. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Every septic company doing home-sale inspections writes reports by hand. I built a clean report builder for one; it works for the whole state."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Septic inspection is the same checklist everywhere, and the first client paid for the build.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Give every member septic company a site template with a pump-out request, inspection page and registration display."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: These associations are small, active and keen to raise members' standing with county regulators.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The septic tank or treatment unit manufacturer
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Owners and builders ask who installs your septic tanks and units locally. A locator with a request form for each installer answers it."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Manufacturers depend on installers and have channel budgets but no trade-specific build.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: County health department septic owner pages
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your septic owners don't know how often to pump or how to find a registered pumper. A plain owner's page with a registered list fixes that."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Counties want fewer failing systems and have outreach money, and a working septic client is proof you know the subject.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Septic site template for rural agencies
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Rural marketing agencies get asked for septic sites and have nothing ready. License my template with the pump-out and inspection pages built."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Agencies serving rural counties lack trade templates and will pay to skip the build.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your agents lose closings to late septic inspections. A member guide with timelines and a directory of inspecting septic firms prevents that."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Associations want to protect deals, and the septic client becomes a featured inspector.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Sewer lateral programs for small cities
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Homeowners don't know they own the sewer line up to the main. A city page explaining it, with a list of licensed sewer contractors, cuts the confused calls."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Public works fields the same lateral questions daily, and the sewer client is your proof of expertise.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Rural water and septic bundle for land developers
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Developers selling rural lots need a page per lot showing perc results, septic options and well notes. I've built the septic side already."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Developers sell lots faster when buyers understand the septic path, and they have budgets.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Septic franchise or multi-truck group pages
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The septic franchise or regional group, per location
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "A septic group with trucks in several counties needs a page per yard with its own townships and pump-out request routing."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: One septic template becomes many locations.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Pump-out reminder service for septic companies
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: Septic companies outside your area, monthly
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "A ready-made pump-out reminder system any septic company can load its customer list into and start booking repeat work."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Every pumper has the same untapped list of past customers, so it sells without custom work.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Septic company in the next county
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: A septic company in a new county
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "I build for one septic outfit per county. {City}'s is taken; the next county's best pumper and installer isn't."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Septic firms are territorial, so exclusivity sells, and the septic demo carries straight over.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Campground and venue septic service agreements
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: Campground and venue owners, via the septic client
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "A service agreement page for campgrounds, venues and farms with high septic loads, with seasonal pump schedules built in."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Commercial rural accounts are steady septic work, and a proper agreement page makes the client look ready for them.

upsellLadder.line: "Your septic site and the care plan go on one contract, so adding a township or a new fee is a text to me."

upsellLadder.trigger: The first pump-out or inspection booked through the site.
upsellLadder.line: "That first online septic booking deserves a review. Let's ask every customer the evening the lids go back on."

upsellLadder.trigger: A realtor books a septic inspection through the site.
upsellLadder.line: "A realtor just booked online. Let's put the septic inspection packet in front of every agent in the county."

upsellLadder.trigger: They mention a backlog of past customers who haven't pumped in years.
upsellLadder.line: "Those past septic customers are overdue. Let's text each one when their tank is due and fill the slow weeks."

upsellLadder.trigger: They say they write inspection reports at night after the truck is parked.
upsellLadder.line: "You're writing septic reports after dark. This finishes them on the phone in the yard."

upsellLadder.trigger: A new driver joins, or they mention probing a yard for an hour to find a lid.
upsellLadder.line: "New driver, same buried lids. Let's pin every septic tank on a map so nobody digs blind again."

upsellLadder.trigger: They add a second pump truck.
upsellLadder.line: "Two septic trucks crossing the county is fuel burned. Let's plan each day by road and disposal site."
